near_miss.lead: Father and mother in genealogical kinship chains
near_miss.why_not: Cognate kin terms occur, but the Irish killing-and-reparation list and Norse pedigree have no distinctive common phrase beyond ordinary descent relationships.

near_miss.lead: Alive/dead opposition: béo no a marb and amṛtasya / jīvati
near_miss.why_not: Corpus search confirms Irish life/death oppositions occur widely, but the epic anchor says a wrongdoer cannot live while the husband is alive. It has no coordinated alive-or-dead capture formula. Cognate life/death vocabulary alone does not establish inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Mother and father as a paired totality
near_miss.why_not: Ordinary parent coordination, with different syntactic functions: parents watching a game; divine titles; protection against a newborn; death from plague. Corpus search finds parent pairs in annalistic and narrative prose as well. No distinctive common poetic function.

near_miss.lead: Father, mother and grandfather in ancestry
near_miss.why_not: The Irish expulsion curse invokes ancestral origin; epic examples concern ascetic parents and grieving as for parents. These contexts do not preserve the same formula.

near_miss.lead: Parent pair and separation from the family
near_miss.why_not: The Irish threat of disfigurement before parents/foster-parents is unlike homecoming, soldierly renunciation, and the Armenian Genesis quotation. The latter is transmitted biblical wording; ordinary father/mother coordination does not resolve inheritance.

Irish déra with adverbial co tróm falcmur describes grief at remembering Finn; Plautus largus lacrumarum describes a threatened expulsion of a lover. Only the tear noun is securely cognate. Wider Irish occurrences show local recurrent diction, not the same modifier or syntactic figure across branches.

Irish at-ibhestar and uisci beside Greek ἔπινον/ὕδωρ or ἐπίνετο/ὕδωρ constitute the ordinary action and its object. Healing/magical sprinkling differs from thirst during siege and massacre. No diagnostic epithet, figure, or inherited ritual context.

near_miss.lead: Parents paired in a social enumeration
near_miss.why_not: Division of remuneration among father, mother and poets differs from the parents-and-companions naming formula in the Odyssey; the cognate kin pair alone is generic.

near_miss.lead: Bring someone back alive or dead
near_miss.why_not: Irish repeats the live-or-dead capture alternative, but the Sanskrit partner explains deaths through Time and has no corresponding alternative or bringing construction.

near_miss.lead: Drink water with cognate verb and noun
near_miss.why_not: Greek personifies irrigated earth as drinking water, whereas Irish describes literal drinking from a cup. The marked metaphor is missing on the Irish side.
Christian release of parents and lord from punishment, Norse descent, and Vedic three mothers/three fathers have unlike functions. The distinctive Vedic number and riddle are absent from Irish.

near_miss.lead: Hound pursuing a deer; dog/deer contrast
near_miss.why_not: Celtic and Homeric corpus searches locate actual Irish hunting and Homeric similes (also Il. 15.271–272). Irish eilit is the accusative object of seeing, conuibh the dative plural after ar, and cú nominative in a hearing clause; the pursuit is subsequent context. Homer has a dog pursuing a fawn, or dog-eyes/deer-heart as insult. Shared animal nouns and ordinary hunting do not preserve a distinctive common collocation or poetic function.
Irish míl denotes game/beasts supplied by a magical dog, whereas Homeric μῆλα are livestock guarded by dogs from predators. The actual relation is different; animal vocabulary is insufficient.

near_miss.why_not: The Irish seven-tongue boast is distinctive, but neither the Lucretian eye/door passage nor the Atharvan earth passage supplies this figure. No different-branch slab anchor for the boast.
